problem.title: Card-fraud scoring service
problem.context: A payments company scores card transactions before authorization at 3,000 TPS normally and up to 15,000 TPS at seasonal peaks. Fraud patterns change within weeks, while confirmed chargeback labels arrive days to weeks later. Auditors may ask months later why a score was produced. Five data scientists, two ML engineers, and the operations team must build and run the system without a dedicated ML platform team.

requirements.text: Score every card transaction before the authorization decision, using the cardholder's recent activity (for example, the spending of the last hour and the last day).
Update the model as new confirmed fraud cases arrive.
For any past score, show which model version and which input values produced it.
During a seasonal peak of 15,000 transactions per second, a score comes back within 30 ms at the 99th percentile.
When the scoring service or one of its data sources fails, authorizations go on. The business accepts weaker fraud detection for up to 15 minutes, but no authorization may fail because of scoring.
An auditor asks about a score from up to 13 months ago. Within one working day the team answers with the model version, the input values and the training data that model was built from.
When the fraud loss rate rises in one segment, a retrained model can be in production within 48 hours, after it has been compared with the current model on recent transactions.
Card data must stay inside the company's PCI-certified environment: no external service may process it.
Seven people build and run the system, with no dedicated ML platform team.

approaches.idea: What if a stateless scorer and local rolling feature cache keep the authorization path short while batch promotion keeps model operations understandable?
What if a replayable streaming topology owns feature computation and scoring so state and decisions share one ordered event history?
What if a transactional database remains the center of feature, score, and training state to minimize the number of systems?
approaches.dropped_because: Per-transaction synchronous SQL aggregation creates a shared latency and availability bottleneck at the 15,000 TPS peak.

approaches.idea: What if the cached scoring path is made easier for the existing operations team through managed PCI-local components and explicit state recovery?

trajectory.hypothesis: Local features should help R1 and Q1; fail-open fallback should satisfy Q2, while durable decision inputs and model snapshots support R3 and Q3. Manual promotion may make Q4 slower.
trajectory.observation: The hot path and retained records look suitable, but a default feature policy needs careful calibration and manual review may consume the 48-hour release window.

trajectory.hypothesis: Partitioned state and scoring should meet R1 and Q1; replayable history should support R3/Q3, and automated guarded retraining should improve Q4. Replication and fallback target Q2.
trajectory.observation: This covers the scenarios well, but a streaming platform and automated release path impose a larger operating and ownership burden on seven people.

values: Scoring path: Synchronous relational database and application scoring

trajectory.hypothesis: Using one database may simplify the small team's operations and recordkeeping, but synchronous feature queries may miss Q1 and Q2 under peak load or database failure.
trajectory.observation: Avoiding extra systems does not offset the per-score SQL bottleneck; the design misses two stressed requirements and its database lineage is not enough to identify training snapshots reliably.

adrs.title: Where scoring and recent activity are computed
adrs.context: The authorization path must combine recent cardholder activity with a score under a 30 ms peak p99, while source or scorer failure must not stop authorization. A short local read path helps latency; durable partitioned processing improves recovery but adds runtime complexity.

options.name: Local cached scorer
values: Scoring path: Stateless service with local feature cache
Recent-activity state: Kafka-fed in-memory rolling aggregates
pros: Local reads support a short scoring path.
Scorers can use bounded-staleness features during source disruption.
cons: Cache freshness and rebuild behavior need operational monitoring.
options.reason: This keeps the authorization hot path small and gives the operations team a familiar recovery boundary.

options.name: Partitioned stream scoring
values: Scoring path: Stateful stream processor scores transactions
Recent-activity state: Partitioned streaming state with durable event replay
pros: Feature updates and scoring share a partitioned event flow.
cons: The streaming runtime increases the team's operating surface.
options.reason: This favors a unified event-driven path and replay for the latency and recovery requirements.

options.name: Synchronous SQL scoring
values: Scoring path: Synchronous relational database and application scoring
Recent-activity state: Transactional SQL aggregates queried per score
pros: One transactional store simplifies some data management.
cons: Per-score queries couple peak latency and availability to the database.
options.reason: It misses the stressed latency and failure scenarios at the required throughput.

adrs.title: How models are updated and compared
adrs.context: Confirmed labels arrive late, but a segment loss increase should lead to a compared model in production within 48 hours. Review and comparison protect against regressions; a release process that waits too long can miss the adaptation window.

options.name: Frequent scheduled guarded release
values: Model release: Frequent scheduled retraining with shadow comparison and guarded promotion
pros: Regularly incorporates arriving labels with explicit shadow comparison.
The cadence and promotion gate are straightforward for a small team.
cons: A schedule can add delay after a segment-specific signal.
options.reason: This balances a reviewable release process with a frequent update cadence.

options.name: Event-triggered automated guarded release
values: Model release: Event-triggered retraining with automated shadow evaluation and guarded promotion
pros: A segment signal can start the retraining and comparison cycle promptly.
cons: Automated orchestration and safeguards require ownership and monitoring.
options.reason: This favors the 48-hour adaptation target when the team can support automation.

options.name: Manual scheduled promotion
values: Model release: Scheduled batch retraining with manual promotion
pros: Manual review keeps promotion decisions explicit.
cons: The schedule and manual handoff can delay a response.
options.reason: The seed's manual release path did not sufficiently address the adaptation target.

adrs.title: How score and training lineage are retained
adrs.context: An answer months later must identify exact model and input values, as well as the training data behind that model. Retention must be durable and practical to query within one working day.

options.name: Immutable decision records and training snapshots
values: Audit record: Immutable score and feature records with versioned training snapshots
pros: Decision inputs and model training snapshots have explicit version identities.
cons: The company must govern retention and access for a large record volume.
options.reason: This directly records the fields the auditor asks for and retains their training lineage.

options.name: Event log with content-addressed manifests
values: Audit record: Durable event log plus content-addressed model and dataset manifests
pros: Durable events and manifests link outcomes to immutable artifacts.
cons: Reconstructing a query may require more specialized tooling.
options.reason: This supports replay and exact artifact identification from the same durable history.

options.name: Database rows and retained tables
values: Audit record: Database score rows and retained training tables
pros: Records can be queried from a central database.
cons: Mutable tables and unspecified snapshot identity weaken exact training lineage.
options.reason: The seed did not establish a sufficiently reliable link from a past score to its training data.

adrs.title: How failures, deployment, and state recovery are handled
adrs.context: Authorization must continue during scorer or source failures, all card data must remain in the PCI environment, and seven people without a platform team must operate the service. Redundancy and explicit recovery help continuity, while additional components increase the operating load.

options.name: Cached path with bounded staleness and replay recovery
values: Failure behavior: Fail open with last-known model and bounded-staleness features
Deployment: PCI-local managed components operated by the existing infrastructure team
Feature recovery: Rebuild aggregates from retained transaction events
pros: Authorization can continue with a known model and bounded feature age.
Managed PCI-local components and replay make recovery supportable.
cons: Fraud detection weakens during degraded operation and scheduled model updates may lag.
options.reason: This gives a defined fail-open path and recovery process within the team's operational capacity.

options.name: Replicated stream path with bounded staleness and replay recovery
values: Failure behavior: Fail open using replicated state and last-known model with bounded-staleness features
Deployment: PCI-local managed components operated by the existing infrastructure team
Feature recovery: Rebuild aggregates from retained transaction events
pros: Replicated state and replay support continuity and reconstruction.
Managed PCI-local hosting satisfies data locality.
cons: The team retains greater responsibility for stream processing and automated release operations.
options.reason: This prioritizes replay and replicated continuity while keeping data within the PCI boundary.

options.name: Fixed low-risk score on failure
values: Failure behavior: Fail open with a fixed low-risk score
pros: The fallback is simple and can avoid blocking authorization.
cons: It abandons useful recent features and may sharply weaken detection.
options.reason: The fallback is too blunt compared with bounded-staleness state and last-known model operation.
